pages.text:
Statistics in design
If a dating site were designed from the theory that ‘similarity attracts,’ the AI algorithm would look for 
the intersection of features between two data sets (one set for each candidate). The potential friends 
the algorithm would come up with would be people ‘just like you:’ same age, ethnicity, social-
economic status, hobbies, character. It would confirm who you are
If the site were designed from a theory of ‘looking for my better half’, it would not focus on similarity 
but on all the distinctive features in the data sets that are assessed as ‘positive’. In other words, the 
better-half algorithm does not look for people who are the same but looks for whom is 
complementing you
Without knowing what an algorithm actually analyses, one could do all the wrong recommendations. 
Should we do the ‘similarity-attracts’ algorithm, then, or the ‘better-half’? Or mixes of both? And 
what ratio between similarity and dissimilarity should be maintained? In addition, do we assume that 
features are either positive or negative (crisp data sets) or can a good quality have a bad side as well 
(fuzzy data sets)? All of these are design decisions that determine what solution a designer offers to a 
client. That is why we do research
Why we do research
3/70

02 How to build up a theory 
5/70
Many people start from a topic and jump straight away into the method but forget to say 
what they are looking for. Data do not give an answer unless you have a question
For example, someone wants to know the user experience of Augmented Reality (AR) in a 
public space and they put an electrode cap on people’s head and measure their brain waves
The question these researchers forgot to ask is:
- What does user experience consist of? What is it?
- How important is physiology in experience? Maybe just run a questionnaire?
- Which components in the electro-cortical substrate are sensitive to AR?
For that, you need to study the literature first
How I feel about 
the exhibition? 
How do you think 
I feel…

●Literature search
Choose your sources carefully, much is unreliable
Due to publish-or-perish culture as well as business sponsoring:
- Predatory journals and conferences (check out Beall’s list at https://beallslist.net/)
- Peer review in the old boy network
- Faked data (e.g., copying photos of stem cells instead of cloning stem cells)
- p-hacking (i.e., manipulating data and analysis such that significance levels are met)
- Honest mistakes (e.g., so-called Type 1 and Type 2 errors)
† Google Scholar maintains no criteria of what is academic or scientific
† Google Scholar relies on metadata, not on content
† Google Scholar does not offer comprehensive results on your topic of interest
† LLMs do not discern ripe from green, fact from fraud
† LLMs combine newspaper articles and blogs with sound science
† LLM sources cannot be traced back (what is that ‘ground truth’?)
That’s why you are taking this course, we separate the silly from the sage
6/70

●Literature search
Apart from Google Scholar, also consult MetaSearch, PSYCHinfo/APA PsychNet, ACM Digital Library, 
IEEE Xplore, CSA Illumina (ProQuest), PubMed
http://www.apa.org/psycinfo/; http://www.apa.org/pubs/databases/psycinfo/
http://portal.acm.org/dl.cfm
https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/Xplore/home.jsp
http://www.proquest.com/
http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/query.fcgi
Note that not all articles have the same value. From strongest to weakest:
1. Meta-analysis (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meta-analysis)
2. Literature review (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systematic_review)
3. Quantitative studies (e.g., a lab experiment, data mining)
4. Case studies (N = 1) (e.g., in-depth analysis of one person or group)
5. Qualitative studies (e.g., an interview, focus group, a philosophical monography)
6. Non-scientific materials (e.g., newspapers, blogs, or unverifiable anecdotes)
Tip: If meta-analyses and literature reviews are in short supply, compensate with more 
of the other types of study (e.g., experimental lab studies and some big-data analysis)
7/70

●Writing an Introduction (= theory)
1. An Introduction starts with an outline of the topic, an example, cites a study, poses a question
2. Based on 1, Introduction makes a statement
3. There is a Figure with the argument structure
4. The Figure shows independent arguments to support the statement
5. Arguments are supported by scientific studies (observe their strength: meta-analysis, case study)
6. Author-year convention followed, proper citation and references provided
7. Structure chosen (e.g., next slide) is consequently followed, visible in the text headings
8. The Introduction ends on a conclusion that synthesises the intermediary conclusions
9. From that, the Research Question follows
10. From the Research Question, hypotheses are derived
In the Tutorial (third hour), we are going to practice this

Research Question
No matter what, all research starts with a Research Question (RQ), which guides you 
through the whole research process. It is the thing you fall back on when you are stuck or 
are digressing; it keeps you on topic
Formulating an RQ
What does it mean to…
• State the general topic
to understand humans
• Narrow down the topic through desktop research
human language
• Question the existing answers
not just syntax and semantics
• Find the research gap
multimodal interaction
• Reformulate the RQ
pragmatics of language use
Science = know why: knowledge 
for its own sake (don’t ask about 
usefulness)
Design/engineering = know how: 
knowledge to make things work 
(e.g., a programme to understand 
humans)

Hypotheses
Derived from the RQ, a hypothesis is a precise problem statement about a 
topic (e.g., about a physical system, a computer system, human experience)
• States the expected statistical relationship between groups of data
• The statement has to be precise and state what we will be measuring!
Not precise enough (what does ‘better’ mean here?):
- Humans are better than AI
- iPhone is better than Blackberry
A little better:
- Humans are more intelligent than AI
- The iPhone keyboard is faster to type on
than the Blackberry keyboard
Most precise:
- Humans have higher scores on standardised IQ tests than does AI
- Users take less time (measured in seconds) to enter in text messages
on the iPhone keyboard than on a Blackberry keyboard
Blackberry had a physical keyboard

The Null and the Alternative hypothesis: H0 and HA
The hypotheses we formulate are commonly about expected effects
• Statements about effects are statements about differences, about change:
- Before-after treatment (medication, washing powder, robot intervention)
- With FinTech, handling your finance is easier than ever
- My GPU is faster than yours
- Assassin’s Creed provokes more intensive emotions than Mario Kart
• That means that there must be at least two sets of data (else, nothing to compare)
• It also means that there must be at least two hypotheses:
H0
There is no effect
The Null hypothesis (no detectable differences)
HA
There is an effect
The Alternative hypothesis (also called H1)
• H0 predicts that differences between two sets of data are statistically not significant
• HA predicts that differences between two sets of data are statistically significant
In Lecture 09 and 10, we will get back to hypothesis testing and discuss what ‘significant’ means 
as it is the researcher deciding when an effect counts or not, based on current knowledge, test 
theory, mathematical approach, application value, and much more

Independent variables or ‘fixed factors’
The condition under which a task is performed is the independent variable (e.g., game 
type, telephone brand, learning with or without VR support)
• Factors that are systematically varied, manipulated, and controlled by the researcher
• Determines a modification to the conditions that people or physical objects undergo 
May also arise from demographic data (e.g., education level, gender, or age)
“Women remember more items after 20 minutes browsing the web than men”
“Older adults report higher satisfaction with a companion robot than do youngsters”
“Compared to Mario Kart, the learning curve for AC is steeper for newbies than for hardcore gamers”
Basim. Assassin’s Creed Mirage, Ubisoft (2023)

Dependent variables or ‘measures’
Measurements (often quantitative)
• The things that we set out to measure/observe (e.g., temperature, time, a rating)
• Demonstrate the effect of the independent variables (e.g., fun while gaming)
• Depends upon the independents as well as the user’s behaviour or performance
Properties
• Readily observable and readily related to some scale of measurement
• Stable and reliable so they do not vary under constant (experimental) conditions
• Sensitive to the effects of the independent variables
Examples: Number of errors made, time taken to complete a given task, time taken to recover 
from an error, attitude indicated on a rating scale
A dependent variable is the variable that changes as a result of the independent 
variable manipulation. It’s the outcome you’re interested in measuring, and it 
“depends” on your independent variable

Dependent variables: qualitative, quantitative
Tests may generate qualitative (i.e., strings) and quantitative data (i.e., integers)
Qualitative evaluation
– Measurements are more subjective and relative (anecdotal)
– Gives us cases, data are less structured, more diverse, or ‘rich’
Quantitative evaluation
– Measurements are more precise and less subjective
– Gives us better controllable results, usually more structured, more uniform, but 
less ‘rich’
– More formal data, allowing for statistical analyses
Typical conclusions after statistical analysis:
“On average, it took users 30% less time to finish a transaction, using FinTech.”

your particular case. Quantitative tests are numerical 
(e.g., speed, accuracy) and may be generalised over 
multiple cases
You must always start from formulating a Research 
Question and derive Hypotheses from it
Only now can you go into method, determining what you 
will measure
Behavioural: Questionnaires, eye-tracking, RT
Physiological: ECG, EEG, fMRI, Galvanic skin response
The Null predicts there is no noticeable difference 
between two sets of data (e.g., Mac vs PC use): effects 
are statistically not significant. The Alternative does 
predict a difference: the difference is significant beyond 
reasonable doubt
